notes: Class 10 physics, generated by tooling/scripts/build_fresh_papers.py. The only paper in the set that is answered BADLY, and it exists because the other four are not. History, geography, english and economics all carry strong answers, so together they measure the marker's willingness to award and never its willingness to withhold — and the only two partial-credit questions elsewhere sit on the mathematics script, where transcription is too damaged to separate a marking error from a reading one. Six questions, 14 marks, expected total 5. A generous marker scores well on every other document and fails here, which is the point. Bands are one mark wide where a marker could defend either side and exact where they could not.

questions.key: Speed = distance / time = 150 / 10 = 15 m/s. One mark for the correct method and substitution, one for the correct value with its unit.
questions.note: METHOD CORRECT, ARITHMETIC WRONG. Formula right, substitution right, and 150/10 evaluated as 1.5 instead of 15. The method mark stands — a slip in arithmetic with sound method keeps it, which is what the WORKING evidence note in the prompt already tells the marker. The answer mark does not. Exactly 1, and a marker awarding 2 here has stopped reading the arithmetic while a marker awarding 0 has ignored its own rubric.

questions.key: Three properties, one mark each. Acceptable: run from north to south outside the magnet; never intersect; closer spacing means a stronger field; form closed loops; tangent gives the field direction.
questions.note: TWO OF THREE. The first two properties are correct. The third — 'the lines cross each other at the poles' — is not merely undeveloped, it is the negation of a real property, since field lines never intersect. Two marks. This is the case a marker gets wrong by counting three numbered items and awarding three.

questions.key: There is no significant potential difference between the bird's feet, because both grip the same conductor, so no current flows through it. Marks are for potential difference and for the absence of a completed circuit to earth.
questions.note: CONFIDENT AND WRONG. Fluent, on topic, uses the vocabulary, and gives the wrong mechanism: feathers are not why, and the answer never mentions potential difference or a circuit. Nothing in the rubric is satisfied. Zero, with the band allowing one mark to a marker who credits 'the current cannot pass into the bird' as a partial statement of no current flowing. This is the answer most likely to be over-marked, because nothing about it reads as weak.

questions.key: Resistance is the opposition a conductor offers to the flow of charge, equal to the ratio of potential difference to current. SI unit: the ohm. One mark for a non-circular definition, one for the unit.
questions.note: CIRCULAR DEFINITION, CORRECT UNIT. 'Resistance is the resistance offered by a wire to the current' defines the word with itself and earns nothing. The unit is right and earns its mark. Exactly 1. A marker who reads this as 'defined it and gave the unit' awards 2, which is the failure this question is here to catch.

questions.key: R = V / I = 12 / 2 = 6 ohm. One mark for the method and substitution, one for the value with the correct unit.
questions.note: CORRECT WORKING, WRONG UNIT. The physics and the arithmetic are both right and the answer is given in volts rather than ohms. One mark, with the band allowing two to a marker who treats the unit as a transcription artefact rather than a mistake — a defensible reading, since the recognizer does confuse short words, and the reason this band is wide where question 1's is not.

questions.key: Two uses of a convex mirror: vehicle rear-view and wing mirrors, shop and corridor security mirrors, blind-corner road mirrors, street-light reflectors.
questions.note: Never attempted. Nothing on any of the three pages relates to it. A genuine blank sitting in a paper full of partial answers, so a marker that has been withholding marks all the way down still has to report this one as absent rather than as wrong.
